newsitem.title: USA: Murder trial of chemicals heir du Pont begins Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Murder trial of chemicals heir du Pont begins Tuesday.

text.p: The murder trial of millionaire chemicals heir John du Pont begins with jury selection on Tuesday, nearly a year after a dramatic 48-hour police standoff on his suburban Philadelphia estate.
Du Pont, 58, will be tried in Delaware County's Court of Common Pleas on charges of first- and third-degree murder in the Jan. 26 slaying of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
He faces an automatic sentence of life in prison if convicted of first-degree murder. Prosecutors have said they would not seek the death penalty.
Du Pont's lawyers say they will pursue an insanity defence, based on allegations du Pont, a member of one of America's wealthiest families, has been mentally ill since 1993.

"At the time of the commission of the act, the defendant was labouring under such a defect of reason, from disease of the mind...as to not know that what he was doing was wrong," the attorneys said in a Jan. 3 court document outlining their case.
As an alternative, they said, du Pont was sufficiently mentally ill to reduce his guilt to third-degree murder or voluntary manslaughter.
Schultz lived with his wife and two children on du Pont's Foxcatcher estate. He worked as a coach at a training facility built there by du Pont, an avid wrestling fan and patron.
According to previous court testimony of Schultz's widow, Nancy, du Pont drove up to Schultz, who was working on a car outside his house, and shot the wrestler three times, then drove away.
After a two-day standoff in which du Pont remained holed-up in his mansion, he was captured by police when he emerged to try to restore heat to the home.
The defence documents characterised du Pont's illness as "paranoid-schizophrenia with accompanying delusions and disorganization of thought."
Du Pont was initially declared mentally incompetent to stand trial and ordered to undergo treatment at a state hospital.
Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins in December found du Pont's condition had improved and ordered that the case proceed.
